title: In every posture
hook: walking, standing, sitting, lying down, keep effort alive (Itivuttaka 110)

segments.voice: Yesterday: parents called by a teacher's title. Your line: show them this world. Today the Itivuttaka follows you through the day, from your feet to your pillow.

Walking to the bus, a grudge shows up. Standing in line for coffee, it's still there. Sitting at your desk, you polish it. Lying in bed at night, you rehearse what you should have said. Four positions, one thought, carried all day like a stone in a shoe. The body changes posture a hundred times a day; the mind often doesn't. One discourse near the end of the Itivuttaka walks through exactly those four positions, and asks what you do with a thought like that in each one.
screen: `A GRUDGE AT THE BUS STOP.` → `STILL THERE IN BED.` → `FOUR POSTURES, ONE THOUGHT.`

segments.voice: Itivuttaka 110 is built like a walk through the day. If, while a monk is walking, a thought of sensual craving, ill will or harming arises, and he puts up with it, doesn't drop it, doesn't drive it out, then, the Buddha says, he is called lazy, lacking ardor. Then the same sentence for standing, for sitting, for lying down awake. Four times, nearly word for word. Then the other side, four times over: if the thought arises while walking and he doesn't tolerate it, but lets it go, dispels it, ends it, he is called ardent, someone whose effort is alive. The Pali tradition counts these four as the postures, iriyapatha, literally ways of moving; other suttas use them to mean all the time. Notice what the text does not say. It doesn't say the thought shouldn't arise. Thoughts of wanting, of anger, of hurting someone come to everyone, monks included. The line is drawn after: do you let it settle in, or see it and set it down? That's a very different standard from never having the thought at all. And notice why the list repeats. Practice isn't only for the cushion. A sitting meditator who spends the walk home nursing a grudge has done one posture out of four. The closing verse pictures someone who keeps at it, walking or standing, sitting or lying down, and says such a one can reach the highest awakening.
screen: `WALKING, STANDING, SITTING, LYING DOWN` · `PUTTING UP WITH IT, OR LETTING IT GO` · `THE THOUGHT ISN'T THE PROBLEM` · `NOT ONLY ON THE CUSHION` · then, large: `IN EVERY POSTURE.`

segments.voice: Notice how you're sitting right now: the weight in the seat, the feet on the floor, the hands, and let the spine lift a little, without strain. Then check the mind the same way: is anything being carried, a worry, a grudge, a wanting? If something is there, don't fight it; see it, the way you saw your posture, and loosen your grip on it a little, the way you'd loosen your shoulders.
Iriyapatha. The four postures, walking, standing, sitting and lying down, in every one of which the sutta asks you not to tolerate a harmful thought.
Your line: effort is alive. The thought may come; what counts is whether you set it down. Day six hundred thirty-three, done.

screen: `DAY 633 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: AS HE SPEAKS, HE DOES.`

howItsDone: Many Buddhist teachers include walking meditation alongside sitting, and some monastic training asks students to keep mindfulness through all four postures, from walking and standing to sitting and lying down.

fork.setup: you're walking, and a thought of ill will toward someone shows up. by Itivuttaka 110's standard, what counts as effort?
options: never having the thought at all.
seeing it and letting it go instead of putting up with it.
waiting until you can sit down to deal with it.
fork.reveal: the text doesn't fault the arising. it calls you ardent for not tolerating it, right there, in whatever posture you're in.

original.note: Pali iriyapatha: a posture, literally a way of moving; the four are walking, standing, sitting, lying down.

trapdoor: what you thought: in every posture means sitting up straight.
what it means: in Itivuttaka 110, keeping effort alive while walking, standing, sitting and lying down, by not tolerating thoughts of craving, ill will or harm.
what a scholar hears: the four iriyapatha recur across the canon, from the posture section of the mindfulness discourses to verses like this one, as shorthand for the whole of waking life.
recall: a book of sayings heard and passed on
guess: a posture, a way of moving

chat.says: If an angry thought pops up while I'm walking, have I failed at practice?
options: No: the text draws the line after, at whether you tolerate it or set it down.
Yes, the text says a real practitioner never has an angry thought at all.
No, the text says only thoughts during sitting meditation really count.
chat.meaning: Itivuttaka 110 doesn't say the thought shouldn't arise. In every posture, it asks whether you put up with it or let it go.

notes: Itivuttaka 110 paraphrased throughout. Confirm the three thoughts (kama-, byapada-, vihimsa-vitakka), the labels for tolerating (anatapi, anottappi, 'lazy, lacking energy') and for dispelling (atapi, 'ardent'), and that 'lying down' is qualified as lying down awake.
Confirm that the closing verse speaks of reaching the highest awakening; it is paraphrased loosely here.
